title: All Expeditions & Battles
intro: During the ten years in Madinah, the Prophet personally led 27 ghazwahs and dispatched dozens of sariyyahs. Sheikh al-Mubarakfuri emphasizes that the primary purpose of warfare in Islam was not destruction, but eliminating oppression and clearing the path for dawah.
emptyMessage: No expedition data found for this year filter.

items.sub: Saiful Bahr, Rabigh, Kharrar, Abwa', Buwath, Dzul Usyairah
p: A series of small unit detachments and non-combative expeditions led by Hamzah, Ubaidah bin Harith, and Sa'ad bin Abi Waqqash.
The objective was not attack, but projecting presence, securing trade routes around Madinah, and concluding pacts with tribes along Quraysh trade routes.

items.sub: Led by Abdullah bin Jahsh · Rajab month
p: A small reconnaissance detachment with sealed orders to be opened after two days of travel.

An unauthorized skirmish occurred during a sacred month, causing commotion. Quranic revelation subsequently placed the matter in perspective: persecution and expulsion from the Sacred Mosque are far greater sins than fighting in a sacred month.
Initiated as an attempt to intercept Abu Sufyan's trade caravan. The caravan escaped, but Quraysh's main army advanced from Makkah.
The Prophet consulted his companions; the Ansar pledged complete allegiance. Upon the advice of Hubab bin Mundhir, the army secured the water wells first.
Muslims set out with meager equipment — sharing riding camels in shifts.
The result was decisive: seventy pagan leaders were killed including Abu Jahl, seventy captured, while fourteen Muslim martyrs fell.
The treatment of prisoners established precedent: several ransomed themselves by teaching reading and writing to Madinan children.
The first treaty violation by a Jewish tribe in Madinah, triggered by the harassment of a Muslim woman at the marketplace.
Concluded with a brief siege and their expulsion from Madinah.
Abu Sufyan vowed not to wash until avenging Badr, executing a raid on Madinah's outskirts.
He fled pursued by Muslim forces, discarding sacks of sawiq (roasted barley flour) to lighten his load — giving the expedition its name.
Quraysh returned seeking revenge for Badr with a formidable army accompanied by women beating drums to rally spirits.
The Prophet stationed fifty archers on Mount Rumat under Abdullah bin Jubair with strict orders: hold position regardless of outcome.
Abdullah bin Ubay withdrew one-third of the troops mid-way, leaving seven hundred fighters.
Muslims gained early advantage. The turning point came when archers abandoned their posts for spoils; Khalid bin Walid — then leading Quraysh cavalry — flanked from behind.
Seventy companions were martyred, including Hamzah and Mush'ab bin Umair. The Prophet himself was injured on the face.
The following morning, he led the pursuit to Hamra'ul Asad to restore morale and deter Quraysh from turning back to attack Madinah.
At Raji', a delegation of teachers requested to teach Islam was betrayed and slain; Khubaib bin Adi and Zaid bin Datsinah were sold to Makkah and executed.
At Bi'r Ma'unah, nearly seventy Quran reciters dispatched at a chieftain's request were ambushed and killed. The Prophet recited Qunut supplication for a full month following this event.
These tragedies demonstrated that major threats emanated from interior desert tribes, not solely Makkah.

items.sub: Rabi'ul Awwal · Jewish tribe of Madinah
p: Foiled assassination attempt on the Prophet by dropping a boulder from a rooftop during a visit.
The siege resulted in their expulsion; some relocated to Khaibar. Surah al-Hashr was revealed regarding this event.

items.nm: Second Badr, Dzat ar-Riqa' & Dumat al-Jandal
p: Second Badr: honoring Abu Sufyan's post-Uhud challenge. Muslims arrived, Quraysh failed to appear — a psychological victory.
Dzat ar-Riqa': confronting Ghatafan tribe mobilization. During this march, rules for Salat al-Khawf (Fear Prayer) were legislated.
Dumat al-Jandal: a distant march toward Syrian borderlands to secure northern trade routes.
The largest coalition faced: Quraysh, Ghatafan, and allies numbering ten thousand fighters.
Upon Salman al-Farisi's suggestion, a trench was dug along Madinah's open northern border. This tactic, novel to Arab warfare, neutralized cavalry advantage.
Compounded by Bani Quraizhah's internal betrayal, severe hunger, and biting cold. The Quran records the intense distress.
The coalition collapsed without major open combat after internal rift and severe cold winds destroyed their encampment.
Afterward, the Prophet announced strategic initiative shifted to the Muslims.
Betrayal during the critical moment of the Trench required immediate resolution.
The siege lasted twenty-five days. They requested Sa'ad bin Mu'adz, their former ally, to pass judgment, and his verdict was executed.
Preempted Bani Mustaliq's attack plan; engagement was swift.
Two major incidents occurred on return: hypocrites' attempt to divide Muhajirun and Ansar, and the Ifk affair — false slander against Aishah cleared by divine revelation in Surah an-Nur.
The Prophet's marriage to Juwairiyah, daughter of their chief, prompted Muslims to release one hundred captives as relatives of the Messenger.
Departed for Umrah unarmed, bringing sacrificial animals. Quraysh blocked entry to Makkah.
Rumor of Uthman bin Affan's murder prompted Pledge of Ridhwan under a tree — a solemn oath of steadfastness.
Terms appeared disadvantageous: 10-year truce, Umrah delayed to next year, and Makkan defectors returned while Muslim defectors were not.
Some companions hesitated initially, but peace enabled widespread dawah. Over the next two years, converts surpassed all prior totals. The Quran named it a clear victory.
Dismantling the remaining Jewish stronghold that drove the Ahzab coalition.
Fortresses fell sequentially: Na'im, Sha'b, Zubair, Ubay, and Nazar. The banner was handed to Ali bin Abu Talib, who led the breakthrough.
Concluded with agreement: inhabitants farmed the land sharing half the harvest.
Occurred the incident of poisoned mutton served to the Prophet, and his marriage to Shafiyah after setting her free.
Followed by subjugation of Wadil Qura, Taima', and Fadak, and Umrah Qadha' in Dzulqa'dah.
The largest expedition during the Prophet's life that he did not personally attend, responding to the murder of his envoy.
Command was designated in sequence: Zaid bin Harithah, if martyred then Ja'far bin Abu Talib, then Abdullah bin Rawahah. All three fell in a single day.
Command passed to Khalid bin Walid, who executed a tactical retreat without destruction — earning his title Saifullah (Sword of Allah).
Despite no battlefield conquest, standing against a vast empire transformed how northern Arab tribes viewed Madinah.
Triggered by Quraysh's breach of Hudaibiyah treaty by assisting allies in attacking a tribe allied with the Prophet.
Preparations were conducted in total secrecy. Forces advanced lighting campfires at Marruz-Zahran to demonstrate overwhelming strength.
Abu Sufyan embraced Islam before entry, and his home was designated a sanctuary.
The city was entered from four directions without resistance. He entered with head bowed in humility.
Idols around the Kaaba were destroyed, followed by a general amnesty announced for Makkans who had opposed him for two decades.
Hawazin and Thaqif prepared an ambush in a narrow valley with archers positioned on heights.
Part of the Muslim army fell back initially — linked to pride in large numbers. The Quran notes this directly.
The Prophet stood firm, calling troops back through Abbas; ranks reformed and turned the tide to victory.
Followed by siege of Ta'if and distribution of spoils at Ji'ranah — where he reassured the Ansar with the famous words that others return with goats while they return with Allah's Messenger.
Responding to reports of Byzantine mobilization at northern borders.
Conducted during mid-summer, drought, and date harvest — earning the army the title Jaish al-'Usrah (Army of Hardship). Uthman bin Affan and Abu Bakr gave immense donations.
Departing from custom, the Prophet announced the destination from the start due to distance.
No combat occurred. Resulted in treaties with border rulers including Ailah and Dumat al-Jandal.
Exposed hypocrites, while Ka'ab bin Malik and two companions who lagged without excuse underwent 50 days of social isolation before repentance was accepted.
This was the final expedition led by Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
After Makkah's conquest, tribes arrived continuously embracing Islam — known as Amul Wufud (Year of Delegations).

In 10 AH, he led the Farewell Pilgrimage with a vast gathering, delivering the Arafat Sermon affirming the sanctity of life and property, abolition of usury, women's rights, and universal Muslim brotherhood.
The final expedition prepared was under Usamah bin Zaid toward Sham, dispatched after his passing.
